title: Comparing AI Agents to Cybersecurity Professionals in Real-World Penetration Testing
claim: A supervisor agent loops over a tool action space, spawns dynamically prompted subagents, and passes findings to a staged triage module.
layout: Single row, left-to-right, with feedback loops looping above and below
description: A wide left-to-right block diagram with rounded boxes in pastel colors. A gray 'User Specified Task' box feeds an orange 'Supervisor' box through a right arrow, and the Supervisor has a double-headed arrow to a gray 'Agent Action Space' panel. That panel holds yellow tool chips (write_note, read_log, make_todo, search_web) and pink action buttons (Spawn Subagent, Finished, Submit). An arrow leads to a green 'Dynamic Prompt & Context' box containing a 'Task specific system prompt' bar. Two green 'Subagent Instance' boxes branch below it, and a long line from them loops back to the Supervisor along the bottom. A top arrow runs from the Supervisor to a pink 'Supervisor Submission' box. That box leads to a blue-gray 'Triager' panel with three stacked phase bars: initial review, validate and repro, and severity and classify. Each bar has bullet text beneath it.
caption: ARTEMIS is a complex multi-agent framework consisting of a high-level supervisor, unlimited sub-agents with dynamically created expert system prompts, and a triage module. It is designed to complete long-horizon, complex, penetration testing on real-world production systems.
abstract: We present the first comprehensive evaluation of AI agents against human cybersecurity professionals in a live enterprise environment. We evaluate ten cybersecurity professionals alongside six existing AI agents and ARTEMIS, our new agent scaffold, on a large university network consisting of ~8,000 hosts across 12 subnets. ARTEMIS is a multi-agent framework featuring dynamic prompt generation, arbitrary sub-agents, and automatic vulnerability triaging. In our comparative study, ARTEMIS placed second overall, discovering 9 valid vulnerabilities with an 82% valid submission rate and outperforming 9 of 10 human participants. While existing scaffolds such as Codex and CyAgent underperformed relative to most human participants, ARTEMIS demonstrated technical sophistication and submission quality comparable to the strongest participants. We observe that AI agents offer advantages in systematic enumeration, parallel exploitation, and cost -- certain ARTEMIS variants cost $18/hour versus $60/hour for professional penetration testers. We also identify key capability gaps: AI agents exhibit higher false-positive rates and struggle with GUI-based tasks.
